status_summary: As of 2026-10-08 the 2022 borrower defense and closed school discharge rules (effective July 2023) are sidelined by statute rather than by ED rulemaking: per the Congressional Research Service, section 85001 of Public Law 119-21 (signed 2025-07-04) provides that for loans originated before 2035-07-01 the 2023 regulations are not in effect and the earlier rules apply (the law's table of contents lists separate headings for sections 85001 and 85002; CRS cites 85001 for both delays and does not mention 85002). ED's own PSLF rule (published 2025-10-31, effective date 2026-07-01) would have let ED end qualifying-employer status for employers it found to have a substantial illegal purpose; on 2026-06-30, before it took effect, the U.S. District Courts for the District of Massachusetts and the District of Columbia each vacated it, the first on a conflict with the statute's definition of public service jobs and the second on the view that the statute gives credit for full-time work at any 501(c)(3) organization, and ED appealed both judgments on 2026-08-27 (CRS Legal Sidebar LSB11472, updated 2026-08-31). Before appealing, ED amended the PSLF application form to remove the employer attestation about a substantial illegal purpose. PSLF itself remains in place (section 82004 of the 2025 law counts Repayment Assistance Plan payments toward it, and ED's 2026-05-01 loan rule confirms this), and no bill ending PSLF or limiting the Secretary's cancellation authority was located.

timeline.event: Executive Order 14235, Restoring Public Service Loan Forgiveness, is signed (the White House page dates it 2025-03-07; ED's 2025-10-31 rule, below, gives the order number). It directs ED to propose revisions to the PSLF regulation so that organizations with a substantial illegal purpose, including aiding immigration violations, do not count as public service employers.

Public Law 119-21 is signed. CRS reports that section 85001 delays the 2022 borrower defense and closed school discharge rules so that, for loans originated before 2035-07-01, the 2023 regulations are not in effect and the prior rules apply, effective on enactment; the law's table of contents lists separate headings for sections 85001 and 85002. CRS also reports that section 82004 counts payments under the new Repayment Assistance Plan as qualifying PSLF payments and that the Act does not otherwise change PSLF. A March 2026 complaint by school-sector plaintiffs describes the same 2035 date and the revival of the 2019 provisions.

ED publishes a final PSLF rule amending 34 CFR 685.219 so that employers with a substantial illegal purpose (including aiding violations of federal immigration law and certain procedures on minors) can be excluded from qualifying employer status, effective 2026-07-01.

ED publishes final regulations implementing the loan provisions of Public Law 119-21 (new loan limits, Repayment Assistance Plan, phase-out of other income-driven plans), effective 2026-07-01; they clarify that Repayment Assistance Plan payments can qualify for PSLF. The portions read did not address borrower defense or closed school discharge.

The U.S. District Courts for the District of Massachusetts and the District of Columbia each vacate the PSLF rule, the day before its effective date (CRS Legal Sidebar LSB11472; captions and docket numbers not given). The Massachusetts court found a clear conflict with the statute's definition of public service jobs (HEA section 455(m)) and rejected ED's reliance on the IRS illegality doctrine; the D.C. court, in a suit by 501(c)(3) organizations, held the statute requires credit for full-time work at any 501(c)(3) organization. A law-firm summary adds that the Massachusetts suit was brought by 22 state attorneys general and also reached First Amendment grounds.

Ninth Circuit denies ED's appeal in the Sweet borrower defense settlement litigation (2016 rule); mandate issued 2026-09-08; class counsel moved on 2026-08-18 to enforce the settlement, with a hearing set for 2026-11-05.

ED appeals both the Massachusetts and the D.C. judgments vacating the PSLF rule; per CRS the appeals remain pending, and ED had first amended the PSLF application form to remove the employer attestation about a substantial illegal purpose.
